paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA).1 The claimant's identity has been established through identity documents filed in evidence.2 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant fears members of the Federal Judicial Police and members of the Gulf Cartel. The claimant alleges that on XXXXX, 2008, he witnessed what he believed to be a drug transaction in a tavern located on a street that divides XXXXX and XXXXX. In the restroom of the tavern, one of the men involved in the transaction threatened the claimant with death if the claimant did not keep his mouth shut. The claimant reported what he witnessed to the Public Ministry the same day. The Public Ministry officials told the claimant that they would investigate his allegations. The claimant started receiving death threats over the telephone on XXXXX, 2008. On XXXXX, 2008, the claimant was assaulted and threatened in his own house by two of the same men he had seen on XXXXX, 2008 involved in the drug transaction and who the claimant believes were Federal Judicial Police officers. The claimant's attackers fled after some neighbours attempted to assist the claimant. The claimant received medical attention for the injuries he sustained in the attack. The following day the claimant reported the attack to the same Public Ministry officials that the claimant reported the first incident to. The officials told the claimant that they would protect him. The following day, the claimant, his wife and two children went to stay with family members in Mexico City. Soon afterwards, the family the claimant was staying with began receiving telephone calls where the caller would ask if the claimant was there. The claimant, his wife and children went to stay with relatives in the city of XXXXX on XXXXX, 2008. Phone calls were made to the claimant's XXXXX residence where the caller would ask for the claimant. An individual also approached the house in XXXXX inquiring about the claimant. The claimant returned to XXXXX on XXXXX, 2008 and stayed for two days. The claimant went to stay in Mexico City on XXXXX, 2008 and fled to Canada on XXXXX, 2008. The claimant filed a claim for refugee protection on March 27, 2009.

I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. The claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason and his removal to Mexico would not subject him personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.

In arriving at my decision, I considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In this regard, I considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Mexico, whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. ANALYSIS State Protection

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. In this regard, the courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.3 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.4

No state is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times and the fact that the state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.5

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy in that state. In a democracy, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action reasonably available to them.6 Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.7

The documentary evidence8 before the Board indicates that Mexico is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is also an independent and impartial judiciary. Having canvassed the country conditions documents,9 I find that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. There is nothing in the documentary evidence before the Board to suggest that Mexico is in a state of complete breakdown.

Furthermore, the Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical, and a complainant can seek redress at a higher level if dissatisfied with the services at the local level.10 According to the documentary evidence11, there are a number of authorities and agencies who will assist members of the public if they believe they have encountered a corrupt official or if they are not satisfied with the services of the security forces.

There is documentary evidence12 that persons who face police misconduct, inefficiency or corruption can ask the Secretariat of the Public Administration (SFP), the Program Against Impunity, or the Office of the Attorney General (PGR) to investigate federal and state police failures or misconduct.

Further documentary evidence indicates that persons seeking redress from corrupt or complicit officials can do so through the National or State Human Rights Commissions and the General Comptroller's Assistance Directorate.13

It is noted that transgressors on the security forces face sanctions, removal, suspension or dismissal. In addition, the Federal Agency of Investigation (AFI) deals with corrupt state officials, drug traffickers and kidnappers.14

Documentary evidence15 indicates that efforts to ensure police effectiveness and purge corruption include investigations by the Secretary of Public Security, complaints monitored by the Inspector General, and a 24-hour hotline to report corrupt officials.

Further documentary evidence16 indicates that the security forces have instituted new recruiting procedures, drug testing, economic incentives, education and certification of officers, with sanctions levied against ineffective or corrupt officers, including arrests, prosecutions and convictions of members of the security forces. The new government laws attacking corruption and bribery have resulted in sentences of five to 10 years' imprisonment for convicted officials, which have reportedly had a marked effect.17

In this particular case, the claimant was questioned as to what efforts he made to seek state protection before fleeing Mexico. The claimant testified that he reported what he believed to be a drug transaction to the Public Ministry the same day he witnessed it. The claimant testified that he reported the incident because he felt it was his civic duty to report suspicious activity that might be drug related. The claimant indicated that President Calderon declared that all Mexican citizens should report any drug activity they see in order to stop narcotics trafficking in Mexico. The claimant also testified that he reported the attack and threats he received at his home on XXXXX, 2008 to the Public Ministry on XXXXX, 2008. The Public Ministry officials told the claimant that they would protect him. The claimant fled to Mexico City on XXXXX, 2008 then fled to XXXXX on XXXXX, 2008 then returned to XXXXX on XXXXX, 2008 for two days then returned to Mexico City on XXXXX, 2008 before fleeing to Canada on XXXXX, 2008. The claimant testified that he did not attempt to follow up with the Public Ministry after his second report to them on XXXXX, 2008 because he had lost faith in the justice system because the justice system had failed to protect him in the past. The claimant went on to describe another incident reported to the Public Ministry years ago when the claimant reported the burglary and ransacking of his home to them. The Public Ministry officials told the claimant to return home and to not disturb anything as the police would be sent out to investigate but the police never showed up. I find that it would be unreasonable for the claimant to expect immediate results from the police following the XXXXX, 2008 incident since the claimant was unable to identify any of the individuals he witnessed involved in an alleged drug deal and only provided the police with a vague description of the men and their vehicle.

The claimant testified that the police showed up at his house on XXXXX, 2008 soon after the attackers fled out the back door. The claimant's attackers then returned and were seen getting into the back of a police vehicle. I find that the police responded to the XXXXX, 2008 assault in a timely manner considering that the claimant was unable to call the police for help himself.

The claimant fled XXXXX one day after reporting the second incident with the Public Ministry. The claimant never followed up with the Public Ministry to check if an investigation was in progress or the status of the investigation if one was in progress.

Claimants are required to show that they sought all avenues of protection reasonably available before seeking international protection.18 In this particular case, the claimant reported the first incident when he witnessed what he thought was a drug deal. The claimant was later threatened four times over the telephone that he would be killed if he made any further reports. The claimant did not report the threatening phone calls. The claimant was later attacked and threatened in his own home which he reported and fled town the following day. I find that the claimant is unreasonable in his expectation of the security forces. The claimant provided the Public Ministry with few and vague details of the individuals involved in the alleged drug deal of XXXXX, 2008 and few and vague details of those who attacked and threatened him on XXXXX, 2008. Furthermore, the claimant fled his city of XXXXX following his report to the Public Ministry on XXXXX, 2008. I find that it would be very difficult for the police to investigate the claimant's allegations provided with such little and vague information and it would be impossible for the police to follow up with the claimant since the claimant was on the move and the police would not know where to find him.

The Board finds that it would be unreasonable to expect in any society that all violent acts reported to police would result in immediate prosecutions or convictions. The Federal Court has held that a claimant's decision to flee before police have had an opportunity to properly respond to and investigate a transgression did not amount to a lack of state protection.19 In this particular case, there is no information to suggest that police were not making genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimant's allegations and apprehend the claimant's perpetrators. Further, I considered the claimant's efforts to report any of this information to any other authority and find that he did not do so.

The panel has considered the documentary evidence20 submitted by counsel with respect to country conditions in Mexico. The Washington Post article entitled "Mexico's drug cartels siphon liquid gold"21 reports on drug traffickers siphoning more than $1 billion worth of oil from Mexico's pipelines in 2008 and 2009. It goes on to say that the authorities have traced much of the oil rustling to the Zetas. However, the same article reports that Mexico has launched an all-out campaign to defend the pipelines, drawing in the army, the Attorney General's office, the Interior Ministry and the customs service. The Washington Post article entitled "Soldiers wary of often corrupt Mexican police"22 reports on Mexico's military confronting corrupt police officers helping the drug cartels. The article states that President Felipe Calderon has acknowledged that corruption permeates Mexico's low paid police at all levels and therefore has opted to combat the billion-dollar drug-smuggling industry by relying primarily on the military which has seen remarkably fewer cases of bribery by traffickers. It goes on to say that his administration also has sent in federal police and soldiers, both of whom are higher paid and usually better educated, to go after police on the take. The same article indicates that Monterrey Mayor Fernando Larrazabal has ordered the city's 1,000 traffic officers off the streets while his administration makes sure they are clean. The officers will undergo polygraph tests and a new citizen-run council will investigate police corruption. Although most of the articles contained in counsel's documentary package describe crimes in Mexico, reports of Mexico's efforts to combat crime and curb corruption are often contained in the same article. In Judith Adler Hellman's "Report on Human Rights in Mexico"23, the author makes statements such as "Mexicans have no recourse to the police for protection from wrongdoers as we do in Canada" and "It basically makes no sense to call on the police to rescue oneself from harm". I find that the author makes general, sweeping statements regarding state protection in Mexico with little empirical data to back up her findings.

I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation24 to indicate that inefficiency, bribery and corruption remain issues in Mexican security forces at all levels, as well as within the public service sector. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists. The preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. I am of the view, in perusing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico.

I am of the view, in perusing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico. The preponderance of the evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic.

I find that the claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of Mexico would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it.

For all these reasons, I find that the claim cannot succeed. There is no objective basis for the claimant's alleged fear, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA, as adequate state protection is available to him.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
